notes: Twin planning JR challenges on telecoms masts; Inspector's Schedule 2 paragraph 5 analysis and alternative sites reasoning are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Planning JR on mobile masts and Telecoms Code powers
key_facts: Two linked section 288 applications challenged inspectors' decisions granting planning permission for Orange PCS mobile phone masts at Winchester and Otterton in Devon.
Local residents objected on health perception, visual impact, and availability of alternative sites including police HQ and railway station car park.
The Winchester challenge focused on whether the Inspector erred in treating Schedule 2 paragraph 5 Telecommunications Code powers as a last-resort compulsory purchase mechanism.
The Otterton challenge concerned alternative sites in an AONB, health perception weight, and the Stewart Report beam zone.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review under section 288 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990, with costs and permission to appeal applications.
enrichment.outcome: Both applications dismissed; permission to appeal refused in each case.
enrichment.ratio: An inspector deciding alternative sites for a telecommunications mast may treat paragraph 5 of Schedule 2 to the Telecommunications Act 1984 as a power of last resort analogous to compulsory acquisition; where landowners such as the police or Network Rail object on operational grounds, it was not Wednesbury unreasonable to conclude that court applications under paragraph 5 would probably fail and that alternative sites were unavailable.
legal_issues: Whether the Inspector misdirected himself on the use of Schedule 2 paragraph 5 Code powers
Whether alternative sites were adequately considered under PPG 8
Whether health perception concerns were properly weighed
Whether the North Star Engineering alternative site required fuller reasoning
linked_authorities: Phillips v Secretary of State [2003] EWHC 2415 (Admin)
Mercury Communications Ltd v London and India Dock Investments Ltd (1993) 69 P&CR 135
Cabletel Surrey and Hampshire Ltd v Brookwood Cemetery Ltd [2002] EWHC 720 (Ch)

confidence.notes: Two linked decisions with explicit outcomes and focused Code powers reasoning; some peripheral health arguments turned on evidence not put to the Inspector.

notes: Wrongful trading and misfeasance claim against RGO directors; detailed fact-finding on Stables funding is extensive and outcome clear.

enrichment.short_title: Wrongful trading claim against Rod Gunner Organisation directors
key_facts: The liquidator of The Rod Gunner Organisation Ltd sought contributions from former directors Roderick and Christopher Gunner for wrongful trading and misfeasance.
RGO traded at a loss from incorporation and relied on funding promises from Jonathan Stables for overheads and a £6 million film production.
By late 1998 Stables had failed to deliver promised letters of credit, BIL facility funding, and other capital injections.
Staff were transferred to a new group company in February 1999 before RGO entered creditors' voluntary liquidation in June 1999.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application by a liquidator for declarations under Insolvency Act 1986 sections 214 and 212 and Companies Act 1985 section 322A.
enrichment.outcome: Declaration granted that the directors are liable to contribute to RGO's assets from 15 October 1998; enquiry directed as to quantum.
enrichment.ratio: Directors may reasonably continue trading and paying salaries while they genuinely and reasonably believe adequate funding will arrive, but by 15 October 1998 the Gunner directors ought to have concluded there was no reasonable prospect of avoiding insolvent liquidation and could not rely on further assurances from Stables or on a proposed NASDAQ flotation of a successor company.
legal_issues: When the directors knew or ought to have concluded insolvent liquidation was unavoidable
Whether continued salary payments after mid-1998 constituted misfeasance
Whether business and goodwill were transferred to G & S for no consideration
Whether section 322A applied to transactions involving connected directors

confidence.notes: Detailed findings on the critical date and section 214 analysis are explicit; transfer and post-February 1999 payment issues were not finally decided.

notes: Neil Lennon libel forum and meaning application; Spiliada principles and meaning ruling are clearly reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Neil Lennon libel: forum stay refused and meaning ruling
key_facts: Neil Lennon sued the Scottish Daily Record over December 2002 articles reporting a Newcastle incident involving Celtic players and a photographer.
The defendant applied to stay the English libel action on forum non conveniens grounds, arguing Scotland was the natural forum.
Over 461,000 copies were sold in Scotland compared with about 22,000 in England, but the claimant had substantial reputation and connections in England.
The articles named three players arrested for robbery but said Lennon was arrested after arguing with police and released without charge.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to stay or dismiss a libel claim, with a preliminary ruling on the range of permissible meanings.
enrichment.outcome: Application for a stay dismissed; the higher pleaded meaning of actual robbery excluded, but the lesser meaning that robbery was highly likely held within the permissible range.
enrichment.ratio: Where a libel is published in England in substantial numbers, England is the natural forum for vindicating English reputation despite much larger Scottish circulation; words reporting named robbery suspects and a separate arrest for arguing with police cannot reasonably bear a meaning that the claimant committed robbery, though a lesser inferential meaning may remain within the generous permissible range.
legal_issues: Whether Scotland was the more appropriate forum under Spiliada principles
Whether the Civil Jurisdiction and Judgments Act 1982 permits intra-UK forum non conveniens stays in libel
What meanings the Daily Record articles were capable of bearing
Whether a modern reader could infer guilt from the text as a whole
linked_authorities: Spiliada Maritime Corporation v Cansulex [1987] AC 460
Cumming v Scottish Daily Record & Sunday Mail Ltd [1995] EMLR 538
Gillick v Brook Advisory Centres
Berezovsky v Forbes [2001] EMLR 45
Jameel v The Wall Street Journal [2003] EWCA Civ 1694

confidence.notes: Forum and meaning outcomes are directly stated; some jurisdictional discussion under the Judgments Regulation was expressly left open.

notes: Social services return-to-Dublin decision upheld on Wednesbury review; children's Act section 20 powers discussed clearly.

enrichment.short_title: JR over offer to return homeless Irish family to Dublin
key_facts: The McDonagh family returned from Dublin to Hounslow in July 2003 claiming racial harassment in Ballyfermot housing.
Hounslow's housing department found them intentionally homeless but provided temporary accommodation while social services assessed the children.
Social services decided the best option was to fund return flights to Dublin, where Dublin City Council would rehouse the family.
The family refused to travel; the council indicated it would consider section 20 duties to the children if necessary.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a local authority decision not to accommodate the family in Hounslow and instead to fund return travel to Ireland.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; costs ordered against the claimants subject to legal aid restrictions.
enrichment.ratio: It was not Wednesbury unreasonable for social services, acting on information that the family were Irish travellers who had left suitable Dublin accommodation without pursuing local remedies, to offer funded return to Ireland while reserving section 20 powers; refusal to return did not make the offer unlawful, provided the authority did not threaten to abandon the children entirely.
legal_issues: Whether requiring a British family to return to Ireland was unreasonable
Whether the council failed in its section 20 Children Act duties
Whether the family’s refusal to travel invalidated the proposed solution
Whether nationality should have been investigated before the decision
index_terms: R v Hammersmith and Fulham LBC ex p Damoah
linked_authorities: R (Ali) v Birmingham City Council [2002] HLR 51
R v Hammersmith and Fulham LBC ex p Damoah (2000) 31 HLR 786
R (G) v Barnet LBC [2003] 3 WLR 1194

confidence.notes: Decision assessed on information available at the time; later nationality evidence and changed circumstances were expressly reserved for fresh review.

notes: Linked planning permission and planning appeal costs challenges; Richards J upheld both inspector decisions with detailed reasoning.

enrichment.short_title: Islington roof extension appeal upheld and costs award sustained
key_facts: Islington refused planning permission for a modern roof extension at 58 Canning Road, N5, citing harm to streetscape under UDP policies D1 and D2A.
An inspector allowed the appeal, relying partly on examples of modern extensions permitted elsewhere in the borough.
The inspector also awarded full appeal costs against the council under Circular 8/93 for unreasonable handling of the application.
The council challenged both the permission decision and the costs award.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 challenge to a planning appeal decision, with linked judicial review of an inspector's costs award.
enrichment.outcome: Section 288 claim dismissed; permission for judicial review of the costs decision granted but substantive review claim dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: An inspector may properly have regard to other modern roof extensions in the borough when judging whether a particular proposal respects local character; a misstatement in one paragraph of a costs decision using 'might' rather than 'would' did not vitiate the overall conclusion that a reasonable authority would have granted permission and avoided the appeal.
legal_issues: Whether comparators from other permitted developments were an irrelevant consideration
Whether the inspector's streetscape conclusions were adequately reasoned
Whether Circular 8/93 Annex 3 paragraph 27 was correctly applied in the costs decision
Whether the costs decision was inconsistent with the planning merits decision
linked_authorities: R v Secretary of State for the Environment ex parte London Borough of Ealing [1999] EWHC Admin 345

confidence.notes: Both linked outcomes and the Circular 8/93 analysis are clearly resolved; costs challenge was heard substantively after permission was granted.

notes: Permission JR on alleged Revenue unfairness refused; Fleet Street Irregulars principles applied straightforwardly.

enrichment.short_title: Capital gains tax JR refused for alleged Revenue unfairness
key_facts: Mr Weston was assessed to capital gains tax on a share and loan note disposal after special commissioners held the loan notes were not qualifying corporate bonds.
He discovered two other taxpayers with allegedly identical transactions were not assessed after Revenue enquiries closed.
All three matters were handled by the same Edinburgh enquiry office, with no explanation for the different treatment.
He sought permission for judicial review alleging unfair discriminatory treatment by the Revenue.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to apply for judicial review after refusal by Charles J, with a pending High Court tax appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Permission refused; the claim held not arguable.
enrichment.ratio: The Revenue's duty to treat taxpayers fairly does not require identical tax charges wherever similar facts appear; the mere fact that one taxpayer was assessed and others were not, without evidence of caprice, favouritism, or discriminatory management, does not establish unfairness or justify judicial review.
legal_issues: Whether differential tax treatment of similarly situated taxpayers is unfair
Application of the Fleet Street Casuals principle to tax enforcement discretion
Whether the Revenue must explain why other taxpayers were not assessed
Relationship between judicial review and the statutory tax appeal process
index_terms: R v IRC ex p National Federation of Self-Employed
linked_authorities: R v Inland Revenue Commissioners, ex parte National Federation of Self-Employed and Small Businesses Ltd [1982] AC 617
R (Wilkinson) v Commissioners of Inland Revenue [2003] EWCA Civ 814

confidence.notes: Permission refusal and unfairness reasoning are explicit; underlying QCB merits were proceeding separately on appeal.

notes: PACE retention appeal after Webb and Costello; detailed statutory analysis and appeal allowed on liability.

enrichment.short_title: Police unlawful retention of seized car parts under PACE
key_facts: Police seized vehicle parts from the claimants' Halesowen unit and a rebuilt car in May 1997 suspecting stolen property.
The claimants were arrested but never charged; items with identification marks were returned but de-marked parts were retained.
The police did not proceed under the Police (Property) Act 1897 after County Court proceedings began in December 1997.
The goods depreciated from about £21,665 to £2,830 before trial in May 2003.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Birmingham County Court on liability for wrongful detention of goods; quantum remitted if appeal succeeded.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on liability; permission to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: Following Webb and Costello, police retention of seized goods after law enforcement purposes under PACE are exhausted requires continuing statutory authority; section 22(2)(b) did not apply where there was no realistic prospect of identifying lawful owners, and section 22(1) cannot justify retention merely because the owner has begun civil proceedings.
legal_issues: Whether PACE section 22 authorised continued retention after criminal investigation ended
Whether the Police (Property) Act 1897 provided ongoing justification
Application of Webb v Chief Constable of Merseyside Police and Costello v Chief Constable of Derbyshire
Whether retention pending County Court trial was 'necessary in all the circumstances'
linked_authorities: Webb v Chief Constable of Merseyside Police [2000] QB 427
Costello v Chief Constable of Derbyshire Constabulary [2001] 1 WLR 1437
Raymond Lyons & Co v Metropolitan Police Commissioner [1975] 1 QB 321
R v Ipswich Magistrates Court ex p Carter [2002] EWHC 332

confidence.notes: Liability outcome and PACE analysis are detailed and unanimous; damages quantum expressly reserved.

notes: Loss Relief GLO jurisdictional ruling; exclusivity of Special Commissioners route explained at length.

enrichment.short_title: Loss Relief GLO: tax appeals not High Court at first instance
key_facts: A Group Litigation Order covered 55 multinational groups challenging UK group relief residence restrictions.
Claimants argued territorial limits in ICTA 1988 conflicted with EC Treaty freedoms and double taxation non-discrimination articles.
Claims combined 'basic group relief' tax issues with consequential restitution and compensation claims.
Marks & Spencer plc had already pursued the core EC law point through Special Commissioners and a High Court reference to the CJEC.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Preliminary jurisdictional hearing in Loss Relief Group Litigation on whether the High Court at first instance could determine basic group relief issues.
enrichment.outcome: High Court held it should not exercise first-instance jurisdiction over basic group relief claims; those issues must begin in Special Commissioners proceedings.
enrichment.ratio: Disputed questions whether group relief was unlawfully denied are co-extensive with adjudicating open or prospective tax assessments and must be determined through the statutory tax appeal machinery beginning with the Special Commissioners, even within a GLO combining basic tax claims with consequential restitution claims.
legal_issues: Whether the High Court has exclusive or discretionary jurisdiction over basic group relief claims
Application of Barraclough v Brown and Glaxo Group Ltd v IRC
Whether a GLO can bypass Special Commissioners jurisdiction
Whether EC law requires a different procedural route
linked_authorities: Barraclough v Brown [1897] AC 615
Glaxo Group Ltd v IRC [1995] STC 1075
R v IRC ex parte Bishopp [1999] STC 531
Marks & Spencer plc v Halsey [2003] STC(SCD) 70
Metallgesellschaft Ltd v IRC (Case C-397/98)

confidence.notes: Jurisdictional ruling is the judgment's sole subject and is fully reasoned; underlying group relief merits were not decided.

notes: CICA legal costs and Human Rights Act challenge; lengthy scheme analysis with appeal dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: Criminal injuries scheme may exclude claimants' legal costs
key_facts: C, severely disabled after assault at 11 months, claimed criminal injuries compensation through her grandparents under a residence order.
The CICA eventually awarded the £500,000 statutory maximum but refused to pay solicitors' costs under paragraph 18 of the 1995 Scheme.
Expert reports were required to quantify care, earning capacity, and equipment needs after a six-year delay in the award.
The claim challenged paragraph 18 as incompatible with articles 6, 8, 14 and article 1 of the First Protocol.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Mitting J on compatibility of the Criminal Injuries Compensation Scheme with Convention rights.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; paragraph 18 held compatible with article 6(1), with medical examination costs recoverable under paragraph 20 where objectively required.
enrichment.ratio: A statutory compensation scheme that excludes representation costs but requires the authority to arrange necessary medical examinations does not deny a fair hearing under article 6(1) where the claimant's access to the scheme is effective and costs can be paid from an eventual award; diminishing the award by legal fees is a policy choice, not a deprivation of the right of access.
legal_issues: Whether paragraph 18 of the Scheme violates article 6 fair trial rights
Whether disabled child claimants are discriminated against under article 14
Scope of paragraph 20 duty to fund necessary medical examinations
Whether article 1 of the First Protocol is engaged by charging costs against the award
linked_authorities: Airey v Ireland (1979) 2 EHRR 305
R (C) v Home Office [2003] EWHC 1295 (QB)

confidence.notes: Article 6 conclusion and paragraph 20 construction are clear; article 14 and article 8 arguments were rejected on distinct grounds.

notes: Large trade mark and passing off appeal with multiple website versions; appeal allowed but form of order remitted and some cross-appeal points remain complex.

enrichment.short_title: Reed trade mark appeal on job advertising use of Reed
key_facts: Reed Employment registered REED in 1986 for employment agency services in class 35.
Reed Business Information and totaljobs.com used Reed in magazine job sections and online recruitment services from 1999.
Pumfrey J found trade mark infringement and passing off across most uses; RBI appealed on identity of services, confusion, own-name defence, metatags, and damages.
The Court of Appeal held later totaljobs versions were not employment agency services and overturned many infringement findings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Partial appeals and cross-appeals from Pumfrey J's liability judgments, with remitted argument on the form of order and costs.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; fresh directions for proposed orders and skeleton arguments, with costs submissions to be renewed.
enrichment.ratio: Trade mark infringement analysis must distinguish Article 5(1)(a) identity cases from Article 5(1)(b) likelihood-of-confusion cases; RBI's searchable online job advertising was not identical to Reed Employment's employment agency services, honest use of a business name may tolerate some confusion, and invisible metatag use did not infringe the REED mark.
legal_issues: Whether RBI's job advertising and totaljobs services were identical to registered employment agency services
Whether there was a likelihood of confusion under section 10(2)
Availability of the own-name defence under section 11(2)
Whether metatag and banner uses constituted trade mark use and passing off
linked_authorities: Gerri v Kelly
BMW AG v Deenik
Premier Luggage v Premier UK
Home Office v Lownds [2002] 1 WLR 2450
Hurst v Leeming [2003] 1 Lloyd's Rep 379

confidence.notes: Core appeal outcome and main infringement reasoning are clear, but multiple website versions and remitted order and costs issues make full enrichment less straightforward.
